cards.beforeWatching: Watch how the brush is filled and how the wash stays even.
observe: Can you repeat a similar stroke twice? Paper texture may break the mark; that is not automatically poor control.
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Wet the brush, load the belly from a small colour puddle and touch it lightly to the palette edge. Make a stroke. If a bead gathers at the end, briefly touch the brush to the cloth before the next stroke. The aim is repeatability, not one universally correct water load.

materials: A small piece of watercolour paper
practice.action: Make six 3×4 cm boxes. Use one pigment and paper; adjust only brush load between rows.
practice.variable: Brush load only; compare repeat strokes before changing it
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Compare the dried edges and any pooling. Record what changed.
practice.reflection: Which brush load and paper condition gave the edge you intended? Describe one visible result and the condition you would repeat.

cards.beforeWatching: Observe the edge difference between a damp and dry surface; do not assume identical spreading on every paper.
observe: Does the damp-paper mark spread farther? Record what happened rather than assuming every paper behaves identically.
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Use one premixed colour for both tests. On one patch of dry paper, place a stroke. Wet a second patch evenly, wait until standing water is gone, then place the same stroke. Note the sheen and the spread. A later, wetter addition can push pigment into a drying area and produce a bloom; that can be useful deliberately.

materials: A small piece of watercolour paper
practice.action: Make two equal strokes with similar paint mixture, one on dry paper and one on evenly damp paper.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: After drying, compare the width and edge softness and note the paper condition.
practice.reflection: Which brush load and paper condition gave the edge you intended? Describe one visible result and the condition you would repeat.

cards.beforeWatching: Observe how the artist chooses large light, middle and dark shapes before detail.
observe: Is the empty paper an intentional light shape?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Draw two small equal rectangles. Mark the largest light and middle shapes, then decide where the dark belongs. Keep paper for the light. Small variations can join one family; this is purposeful simplification, not a claim that the subject has only three tones.

materials: Paper and a soft pencil, or one neutral watercolour
A simple object, view or your own reference
practice.action: Using one pigment, paint three postage-stamp thumbnails with no more than five connected masses.
practice.variable: Arrangement of the large value groups
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Identify intentional paper-white, middle and dark grouping; test hierarchy from arm’s length.
practice.reflection: Which value arrangement better served your intention, and what changed in the viewing experience?

cards.mappingCorrection: Previous candidate was an unrelated brushstrokes video; require actual observed value-grouping sequence.
cards.beforeWatching: Look for where the principal dark and light shapes are grouped, and how that grouping changes the focal emphasis; do not judge value by colour names.
observe: Where does your attention go first, and is that consistent with your intention?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Fill each mass with one family. Let neighbouring masses connect when their values are close. A focal area may be supported by local contrast, isolation or shape; it does not have to be centred or extremely dark.

materials: Paper and a soft pencil, or one neutral watercolour
A simple object, view or your own reference
practice.action: Create two miniature thumbnails of a familiar scene, changing only the dark-mass grouping.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Compare which version supports your intended focal area.
practice.reflection: Which value arrangement better served your intention, and what changed in the viewing experience?

cards.beforeWatching: Observe exactly when the paper is wet or dry and what the second brush is doing.
observe: The edge may spread and change apparent value. Note that limitation rather than pretending the comparison is perfectly controlled.
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Use the same mixture on evenly damp paper for the second shape. Alternatively, on a fresh test, touch one still-wet boundary with a clean damp brush. These are future practice methods, not methods inferred from someone else's painting. More water can travel back into a drying passage and make a bloom.

materials: A small piece of watercolour paper
practice.action: Paint one hard-edged square and one wet-into-damp shape with the same pigment.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: After drying, compare the boundary transitions without calling both “lost edges”.
practice.reflection: Where did an edge remain hard, soften or disappear? Which relationship would serve your chosen style, and why?

cards.mappingCorrection: A softened edge is NOT automatically a lost edge; exercise stands without video.
cards.beforeWatching: Only if an inspected demonstration shows a boundary visually disappearing between similar adjacent values, examine how the form remains legible.
observe: Does the form still read without every contour being stated?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Place a similar-value neighbouring passage beside part of a third shape, allowing the two to meet. Aim for a short boundary to become difficult to distinguish while the rest of the shape still reads. Then make a tiny application with one selected sharper edge and one quieter interval.

materials: A small piece of watercolour paper
practice.action: Connect two similarly valued adjacent shapes and intentionally omit part of their dividing contour.
practice.variable: Presence of part of the shared contour, keeping neighbouring values similar
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Check whether the composition still reads and the shared edge truly disappears.
practice.reflection: Where did an edge remain hard, soften or disappear? Which relationship would serve your chosen style, and why?

cards.beforeWatching: Look for the horizon, vanishing point and actually related edges; not every line must converge.
observe: Which edges describe the same direction in space, and which do not?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Draw a few major edges. Look at their slopes relative to horizontal and vertical. In a conventional linear-perspective description, parallel edges in the same spatial direction may converge toward a shared vanishing point, possibly far outside the page; different directions need not share it.

materials: A box or a simple building viewed from a fixed position
practice.action: Sketch a street corner with observed verticals and two directional groups.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Explain which lines share a direction in 3D and which do not.
practice.reflection: Which relationship did observation change? Was a remaining distortion intentional or something to revisit?

cards.beforeWatching: Observe the order of large masses and whether planned dark areas stay limited.
observe: Does the large organisation serve your intention before colour is added?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Make a tiny pencil plan beside the painting. Decide where the light paper remains, which mass is middle value and where a limited dark can belong. A misty plan can compress the whole range; the darkest area need not be black.

materials: One blue or neutral pigment; an optional familiar earth colour
Pencil, palette, clean water and cloth
practice.action: Draw three large value masses of sky, hill and bank without details.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Read at arm’s length: does the chosen arrangement support quiet atmosphere?
practice.reflection: Which planned relationship survived drying? Name one choice to preserve and one variable to test in a separate study.

cards.beforeWatching: Watch the moisture timing and stopping point rather than imitating a specific cloud contour.
observe: Does the broad light mass remain simple?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Apply the pale mixture across the sky area with a consistent load. Leave intended paper lights. A little variation can be appropriate; avoid repeatedly chasing an even finish as the passage dries.

materials: One blue or neutral pigment; an optional familiar earth colour
Pencil, palette, clean water and cloth
practice.action: Paint two 5×7 cm skies; vary paper moisture and preserve one light passage.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: After drying, compare soft edges, uncontrolled blooms and intentional light space.
practice.reflection: Which planned relationship survived drying? Name one choice to preserve and one variable to test in a separate study.

cards.beforeWatching: Watch the relationship between distant and nearer masses, avoiding a formulaic “distance always lighter”.
observe: Does the hill separate enough to read without taking all the attention?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Use the tested middle mixture for a simple distant hill. For this atmospheric option, let part of its boundary soften into a suitable damp passage. If the sky has dried, use a fresh scrap test rather than scrubbing it back into submission.

materials: One blue or neutral pigment; an optional familiar earth colour
Pencil, palette, clean water and cloth
practice.action: Add a restrained hill wash behind an already dry foreground plan.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Does the hill separate without overpowering the intended focus?
practice.reflection: Which planned relationship survived drying? Name one choice to preserve and one variable to test in a separate study.

cards.mappingCorrection: Supplied card matthew-landscape-2025 conflicts with corrected coverage; use matthew-process-2024 as the research proposal.
cards.beforeWatching: Observe which details are added late and which are deliberately omitted.
observe: Can you explain why your finishing choice helps the stated intention?
Compare the visible condition before and after the mark; do not infer an unseen painting process.
cards.understand: Look at the dry painting. Ask whether the intended landing already reads. If it does, stop. If not, test one small value or edge adjustment on scrap first. More detail is not automatically more resolved.

materials: One blue or neutral pigment; an optional familiar earth colour
Pencil, palette, clean water and cloth
practice.action: Add at most three dark accents to a dry study, one at a time.
constants: Same paper, pigment and viewing distance unless that is the stated variable
success: Does each accent strengthen the intended focus, or create noise?
practice.reflection: Which planned relationship survived drying? Name one choice to preserve and one variable to test in a separate study.
